claims.text: The material under study is Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state.
Exposure to harsh environments can initiate corrosion-related degradation in Q235 steel.
A stable passive layer forms on Q235 steel under the stated exposure conditions.
Formation of a stable passive layer suppresses corrosion-related degradation.
Chromium and molybdenum enhance stable passive-layer formation.
Thermodynamic stability of the passive layer is the governing corrosion-suppression mechanism.
The proposed mechanism suppresses corrosion-related degradation by 20% relative to untreated Q235 steel.
The proposed corrosion-suppression behavior applies at both room and elevated temperatures.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution is an applicable exposure environment.
The magnitude of corrosion suppression depends on environmental conditions and alloy composition.
The proposed experiment varies temperature and environmental conditions while measuring corrosion rate and passive-layer thickness.
An increase in corrosion rate of more than 10% relative to the untreated reference would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes passive-layer enhancement to chromium and molybdenum, but the intervention and controlled study vary only exposure temperature and environment; they neither add nor independently vary Cr or Mo, so the stated experiment cannot isolate the claimed alloying-element cause.
The conditions call for variation of environmental conditions, whereas the boundary specifies only a fixed 3.5 wt.% NaCl environment and does not define which environmental variable will be changed.
